A.explanation: This calculates $f/v$ instead of $v/f$, giving $10/1500$ m and $40/1500$ m which are $6.7\text{ mm}$ to $27\text{ mm}$.

B.explanation: This uses $1.5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ instead of $1500\text{ m s}^{-1}$, missing the km to m conversion, giving $1.5/40$ m to $1.5/10$ m.

C.explanation: These values do not satisfy $v = f\lambda$ with $v = 1500\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and are about a factor of 5 too small.

D.explanation: Using $\lambda = v/f$ gives $1500/40 = 37.5\text{ m}$ and $1500/10 = 150\text{ m}$, about $38\text{ m}$ to $150\text{ m}$.

hints: Convert the wave speed to SI units: $1.5\text{ km s}^{-1} = 1500\text{ m s}^{-1}$ before using it with $10\text{ Hz}$ and $40\text{ Hz}$.
Recall $v = f\lambda$ for a progressive wave, so $\lambda = v/f$ and the higher $40\text{ Hz}$ frequency must give the shorter wavelength.
Calculate $\lambda$ for both ends separately and keep the result in metres, then write the range from the small $40\text{ Hz}$ value to the large $10\text{ Hz}$ value.
walkthrough: Identify the givens: $f = 10\text{ Hz}$ to $40\text{ Hz}$ and $v \approx 1.5\text{ km s}^{-1} = 1500\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in seawater.
State the progressive-wave relation $v = f\lambda$, rearranged to $\lambda = v/f$. Wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency.
For the lowest frequency, which gives the longest wavelength: $\lambda_{max} = 1500/10 = 150\text{ m}$.
For the highest frequency, which gives the shortest wavelength: $\lambda_{min} = 1500/40 = 37.5\text{ m} \approx 38\text{ m}$.
Check units: $(\text{m s}^{-1})/(\text{s}^{-1}) = \text{m}$, so tens to hundreds of metres is sensible for very low frequency sound at high speed.
The range from short to long wavelength is therefore about $38\text{ m}$ to $150\text{ m}$. This is option D.
